replies:
It’s a really common question — and great that you’re thinking about it, because a 2-year-old can indeed seem to see perfectly fine even when there’s an underlying issue. The short answer is: **yes, routine vision screening is recommended for all children, even if they appear to see well.**

Here’s why, and what you can expect.

### Why screen when everything seems normal?

- **Kids can’t always tell you** — A 2-year-old doesn’t know what “normal” vision looks like. If one eye is weaker, they may simply rely on the stronger eye and never complain.
- **Some conditions have no obvious signs** — For example, amblyopia (lazy eye) or mild refractive errors (like nearsightedness) can be silent. You won’t necessarily see squinting, eye rubbing, or head tilting early on.
- **Early detection = better outcomes** — Many childhood vision problems are most treatable during the first few years of life. The window for successfully treating amblyopia, for instance, is much wider before age 7–8. Catching something at age 2 gives a huge head start.
- **Screenings catch more than just “blurry vision”** — They can detect eye misalignment (strabismus), significant differences in prescription between the two eyes, and even serious problems like cataracts or retinoblastoma (though rare).

### What do pediatric guidelines say?

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), American Academy of Ophthalmology, and other major organizations recommend:

- **Vision risk assessment at every well-child visit from birth.**
- **Instrument-based vision screening at ages 1 and 2** (using a handheld device that checks the eye’s focusing power and alignment — no reading letters needed).
- **Formal visual acuity testing starting at age 3 or 4** (when kids can name pictures or letters).

So at age 2, screening is very much part of the standard preventive care schedule. If your child hasn’t had one yet, the next well-child visit is a perfect time to ask.

### What does screening look like at this age?

For a 2-year-old, it’s quick, painless, and non-invasive. Usually the pediatrician or trained staff will use a photoscreening device (like a special camera) that takes a picture of the eye’s red reflex and estimates the shape of the eye. The child just needs to look at the device for a few seconds. No reading required. It’s often done as part of the check-up.

If the screening flags anything, the pediatrician will likely refer you to a pediatric ophthalmologist or optometrist for a more complete eye exam. A referral doesn’t mean there’s definitely a problem — screening tools are designed to be sensitive to catch anything that *might* need treatment.

### “But my child sees tiny crumbs on the floor from across the room!”

Toddlers are amazingly adaptive. You might notice them recognizing small objects or pointing out faraway birds, but what you can’t easily see is:

- How well the eyes work *together* (binocular vision).
- Whether each eye individually is seeing clearly.
- Early changes that will only become obvious when the brain starts to favor one eye.

A child can have 20/20 vision in one eye and very poor vision in the other, yet still function normally because they simply ignore the input from the bad eye. That’s why screening matters.

### Bottom line

Yes — have his vision screened, even though he seems to see fine. It’s a simple, standard part of preventive care at this age. You’re not overreacting or looking for problems; you’re following guidelines that exist precisely because so many issues in young children are invisible to parents.

Bring it up at his 2-year well-child visit (or sooner if one is already due), and your pediatrician can either perform the screening or tell you where to get it done. You’ll walk away either with peace of mind or with a plan to tackle anything early — both are great outcomes.

DO IT
